In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the radio emission from young stellar objects is dominated by optically thin free–free emission, but that this emission is variable and that the variability is likely to be a function of both the evolutionary state of the source and the nature of the outflow.
the radio luminosity of Class 0 and Class I objects is correlated with both bolometric and envelope luminosity, but that the envelope mass provides a more robust correlation.
the radio properties of these sources are broadly consistent with the canonical expectations for Class 0/I objects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the radio luminosity of Class I objects in Serpens is consistent with that of Class I and Class 0 objects in other molecular clouds.

the radio emission of the sources in our sample is likely to be dominated by the stellar winds of the young stellar objects, and that the radio luminosity of these objects is a better indicator of their evolutionary status than the bolometric luminosity.

the low detection rate for the Class I objects, combined with the low spectral index values, indicates that these sources are in an early evolutionary stage, and that envelope mass provides the best indicator for radio emission from these sources.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the AMI-LA is a powerful tool for probing deeply embedded young stellar sources in molecular clouds, and that future observations with the AMI-Low will provide even deeper observations of this region.

the low detection rate of Class I objects in our sample is consistent with a scenario in which the Class I stage is short-lived, and the Class I sources are in a transition between the optically thick Class 0 stage to the optically thin Class II stage.
radio observations of young stellar objects are a valuable probe of their evolution.
